newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian president starts talks on crisis.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian president starts talks on crisis.

text.p: Bulgaria's new president Petar Stoyanov met leaders of warring political factions on Thursday to seek a way out of deadlock blocking formation of a new government.

Stoyanov, who took office on Wednesday, held separate, hour-long meetings with the opposition and leaders of the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), which has the majority in parliament, but there was no immediate sign of a breakthrough.

The constitution requires the president to ask the ex-communist Socialists to form a new government but the opposition has held 16 consecutive days of protests to demand a general election. More rallies are planned later in the day.
Ivan Kostov, leader of the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said he hoped the Socialists would have the sense to decline a mandate in the explosive climate.

"We understand President Stoyanov's constitutional obligations which require him to hand over a mandate to the BSP, but it is obliged to return this mandate because social opinion is against it," he said.

Socialist leader Georgi Parvanov said the Socialists insisted on forming a cabinet led by Interior Minister Nikolai Dobrev, unacceptable to the opposition who blame him for violent clashes between police and demonstrators outside parliament on the night of January 10.
"We do not doubt that we will receive a mandate in a very short period," Parvanov said.

The lev currency, which has been in freefall as the crisis has worsened, hit new lows near 900 to the dollar on the interbank market. The central bank fixing for Thursday was 731.71, compared to 495.74 at the beginning of the year.
The collapse of the lev reduces the value of Bulgaria's huge domestic debt but will drastically increase the cost of grain imports to be needed from next month, and fuel imports.

Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate funding from the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended disbursements because the Socialist government has not implemented previous reform programmes.

As a last resort, the IMF has proposed a strict fixed exchange rate regime which will prevent the government printing money, and has said it is ready to resume negotiations on its implementation as soon as a government is in place.

The Socialists have offered elections in December, a year ahead of schedule, but in the meantime they want to form a new cabinet to take over from prime minister Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21. The UDF wants elections in March.

The BSP leadership on Wednesday approved organisation of potentially explosive counter-rallies, saying they were under pressure from supporters around the country, but a spokeswoman said on Thursday there were no immediate plans to organise such rallies.
